questions.q: In the 2009 eclipse, how long did totality last at Patna, and when did it begin by Indian clocks?
questions.do: Pick 22 July 2009 and Patna under Your eclipse, then read the cards.
questions.a: Totality lasted 3 min 44 s and began at 06:24:39 IST, with the Sun only about 15° above the horizon. This matches the published table to the second.

questions.q: Will Delhi see the 2 August 2027 eclipse? How much of the Sun is covered, and at what time?
questions.do: Pick 2 August 2027 and Delhi. Read Sun covered and Greatest.
questions.a: Only a partial eclipse: about 8% of the Sun covered at about 16:29 IST. Try Mumbai, further west, for a deeper partial eclipse.

questions.q: Why is a ring of fire (annular) eclipse never safe to look at, while totality briefly is?
questions.do: Pick 21 May 2031 and Kochi, slide Moment to the middle, and look at the picture. Then read the warning box.
questions.a: In an annular eclipse the Moon is too far away to cover the whole Sun, so a bright ring of sunlight always remains (here about 92% is covered, not 100%). Only in totality is all of the bright surface hidden.

questions.q: The 1919, 1955, 2009 and 2027 eclipses are all members of one family, Saros 136. How far apart are they in time, and which had the longest totality?
questions.do: Read the table under The family of 2027: Saros 136.
questions.a: Each comes one saros later: 18 years, 11 days and 8 hours. The longest totality is 1955, 7 min 08 s, across Sri Lanka and the Andaman Islands.

questions.q: What did Pierre Janssen discover from Guntur during the eclipse of 18 August 1868, and how long before anyone found it on Earth?
questions.do: Read From Rahu to helium to Aditya-L1.
questions.a: A new yellow line in the Sun’s spectrum: the element helium. Chemists isolated it on Earth in 1895, 27 years later.
